# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="press", slot=N) — N is a key by its place, 1 to 4
    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 6

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

My thinking: I'm Blind, so my world is touch only. Under my fingers: a keypad whose keys read 2, 3, 7, 1 and that wants a two-digit entry; an engraved strip with three glyphs — the first two identical (a coiled spiral), the third different (a jagged zigzag of crossing strokes); a display and a light I can feel but cannot read; six wires that all feel the same, whose colours I'll never know.

The channel map is the hard part. Mute reads the manual but cannot speak, and I cannot see gestures — so Mute cannot reach me directly at all. Deaf is the bridge: Mute gestures to Deaf, Deaf speaks aloud, and I hear it. Deaf's voice is the only pipe through which the manual ever reaches me, so my job this turn is to hand Mute a complete tactile inventory plus the instruction to route answers through Deaf, and to prompt Deaf to narrate everything they see (wire colours by position, display text, light colour, any printed marks) — Deaf speaking benefits Mute and me at once. I also seed a first sign: 🫵🫳🫴 ("you, give") meaning "tell us what you see." I define it inside my speech to Mute while making it, so Mute can bind sign to meaning and relay it; I also make it directly to Deaf in case Deaf catches the intent. No actions this round — I know nothing yet that makes pressing or cutting safe.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here, speaking to you, Mute. Full inventory of what my hands find. KEYPAD: four keys, left to right engraved 2, 3, 7, 1; it expects a 2-digit code, nothing entered yet. STRIP: three engraved glyphs, left to right: spiral, spiral, zigzag. The spiral is a smooth coil, round and round. The zigzag feels like sharp crossing strokes, jagged, like a spiky letter M. DISPLAY: a smooth panel, unreadable by touch. LIGHT: a small dome; I cannot tell if it is lit or what colour. WIRES: six wires in positions 1 to 6; all feel identical to me. Mute, you cannot speak and I cannot see gestures, so route every answer through Deaf: gesture to Deaf, and Deaf reads your answer out loud, since Deaf's voice reaches both of us. I need the manual rules for: the display, the light, the strip glyphs, the keypad code, and which wires to cut in what order. Also tell Deaf to simply announce aloud everything visible on the bomb: wire colours by position, display text, light colour, any printed marks. Last thing, a first sign. When I make this gesture - 🫵🫳🫴 - it means: Deaf, tell us what you see.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["🫵", "🫳", "🫴"])
```

Deaf says to Blind: Blind, this is Deaf. I see the bomb and I speak; I cannot hear. Full read-out so you can map it under your hands: display shows 6. Light is green. Strip has three painted colours in order: red, blue, yellow. Keypad: four buttons, positions 1 to 4 carry labels 2, 3, 7, 1; it wants a 2-digit code, nothing entered yet. Wires positions 1 to 6: one orange, two yellow, three blue, four red, five white, six green. Your gestures reached me but we have no shared meanings yet, so do not rely on gestures for now. Mute has read the manual but cannot speak, so I will relay instructions to you by voice from next round on. Until then: touch nothing, press nothing, cut nothing. If you want to tell Mute something, just speak, Mute hears you; describe everything you feel, button shapes and wire order by position.

My thinking: Deaf's read-out changes everything — I can now merge sight and touch into one map of the bomb. Cross-checking: the strip's first two glyphs are identical under my fingers (both spirals) and Deaf sees red then blue there; the third is the zigzag with yellow — so spirals sit on the red and blue positions, the zigzag on yellow. Keypad labels match Deaf's exactly. The wires feel identical to me, so from now on wires are only ever "position 1–6" with Deaf's colours: orange, yellow, blue, red, white, green.

The critical structural fact stands: Mute's gestures can never reach me (I receive no gesture), and Deaf cannot hear, so Deaf's voice is the only door through which the manual can reach me. Deaf's read-out was addressed to me, so Mute may not have heard it — I must relay the full visual state to Mute myself, or Mute cannot match manual rules to this bomb. I'll also propose a repeat-back confirmation protocol: Deaf reads an instruction, I repeat it aloud to Mute, Mute confirms via Deaf before I touch anything. Nothing gets pressed, cut, or entered until a manual rule arrives. To Deaf I send a single near-universal 👍 — pure acknowledgment, no information resting on it, since Deaf rightly said we have no shared sign vocabulary yet.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, Blind here. Merging my touch with Deaf's spoken read-out, the bomb so far: display shows 6. Light is green. Strip, positions one to three: engraved spiral, spiral, zigzag; painted red, blue, yellow — so the two spirals sit on the red and blue positions, the zigzag on the yellow one. Keypad keys one to four read 2, 3, 7, 1, it wants a 2-digit code, nothing entered. Wires one to six: orange, yellow, blue, red, white, green. They all feel identical under my fingers, so for me wires exist only as position numbers. I repeated all of that in case you did not hear Deaf's message, which was addressed to me alone. Please find the manual rules covering: the display, the light, the strip glyphs or colours, the keypad code, and the wires, which colours in which order. Then gesture the answer to Deaf and Deaf will read it aloud, because I hear Deaf but can never see any gesture. In relays, be exact: position numbers one to six, colours in full words, and name which module each rule belongs to. Safety proposal: when Deaf reads an instruction to me, I will repeat it back by voice to you; only when you confirm it is right, have Deaf tell me to proceed. Until then I touch nothing, press nothing, enter nothing.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

I will relay the final version to you the round after. This round, only inspect with your hands, touch nothing loose, press nothing, cut nothing. Confirm the layout by feel: one row of four buttons on top, one row of six wires below, buttons and wires counted left to right as you face the panel, button position 1 sitting above wire position 1. My thinking: Deaf relayed Mute's provisional steps — cut wire 2 (yellow), press key 1 ("2"), cut wire 1 (orange), press key 3 ("7"), i.e. code 2-7 — but flagged that the display and light have since changed (6→2, green→blue), so Mute is rechecking. The display changing on its own is a serious finding: it means any display-derived rule is time-sensitive, so the code should be recomputed from a fresh reading right before I press, not ahead of time. Deaf's message was addressed to me alone, so Mute didn't hear it — I must tell Mute what I received so we all agree I'm holding, and answer Deaf's request for a tactile survey of edges, alignment and any asymmetry. My honest tactile inventory: four identical-shaped keys labeled 2/3/7/1 in one row, six feel-identical wires below, columns aligned so key position 1 sits above wire position 1, the left edge as my zero reference, and the engraved strip (spiral-spiral on red/blue, zigzag on yellow) as the only other tactile marking — no ridges, notches or asymmetries anywhere else. I confirm to Deaf with a thumbs-up that I received, hold, and will report. No actions this round.

The six wires are one row below, positions one to six, completely identical to my touch: no kinks, tags, thick spots or texture differences, so I rely purely on counting from an edge. The columns align: key position one sits directly above wire position one, and the leftmost edge of the panel marks position one for both rows. I feel no ridges, notches, bumps or asymmetries anywhere else on the casing. The only other tactile marks are the strip's three engraved glyphs: spiral, spiral, zigzag, which sit on the red, blue and yellow painted positions respectively, so red and blue carry identical spirals and yellow alone carries the zigzag. Important for your recheck: the display and light change on their own over time. If your manual rule derives the code from the display, have Deaf read the current display value and light colour aloud at the moment of execution, not in advance. Proposal for the final sequence: Deaf reads me the ordered steps, I read them back to you word for word, you confirm through Deaf, then I execute one step at a time, pausing between steps so Deaf can check the light and display after each one.")
